You are implementing exactly ONE change request in a checkout of the Django web framework (version 3.2 development, Python 3.9).

Your current working directory is an ISOLATED git worktree of the repository. It is a full, working Django source tree. Nobody else is editing it. Work only inside it.

## The change request

Read the file `requirements/parse-duration-negative-days.yaml` in your working directory. It contains `title`, `category` and `requirement` fields. The text is a paraphrase / rewrite of the commit message of a REAL upstream Django commit that was made on top of this exact tree state. Your job is to reproduce that upstream change as faithfully and completely as you can infer it.

## How to work

1. Read the requirement file completely. The title usually contains the upstream ticket ("Fixed #12345 -- ...") and is a strong hint about the affected component.
2. Locate the relevant code. Use `grep -rn`, `Grep`, `Glob` over `django/`, `tests/`, and `docs/`. Read enough surrounding code to understand the existing design and conventions.
3. Implement the change:
   - Change the library source under `django/` when the requirement describes a behaviour/bug/feature change.
   - Update or add tests under `tests/` when the requirement describes testable behaviour, mentions a regression test, or is itself a test-only change. Put tests in the existing test module/class that covers that area; follow its style exactly.
   - Update documentation under `docs/` when the requirement is about docs, deprecations, new public API, or release notes for a new feature/deprecation. Do not invent release notes for plain bug fixes.
   - If the requirement is a pure cleanup/typo/refactor, make exactly that cleanup and nothing more.
4. Match the surrounding code style: same naming, same comment density, same import ordering (isort-compatible), 4-space indent, max line length 119, no trailing whitespace. Django source uses single quotes predominantly.
5. Be complete but MINIMAL and SURGICAL. Do not reformat unrelated code, do not "improve" nearby code, do not bump version numbers, do not touch `AUTHORS`.
6. NEVER modify any of these paths: `requirements/`, `requirement_patches/`, `agent_plans/`, `agent_tests/`, `.claude/`, `Django.egg-info/`. Do not create files at the repository root.
7. Verify. Run the focused tests you touched (and the closest existing suite) like this:
   `cd tests && python3 runtests.py --parallel=1 <label> 2>&1 | tail -30`
   where `<label>` is e.g. `admin_views.test_history_view` or `queries`. Databases available: sqlite (default) only. If a test needs postgres/oracle/mysql it will be skipped — that is fine, but make sure it at least imports and collects. Also byte-compile files you edited: `python3 -m py_compile <files>`.
8. Iterate until the focused tests pass (or are legitimately skipped for lack of a backend).

## Deliverable (MANDATORY)

From the ROOT of your worktree, run exactly:

    git add -A && git diff --cached --binary > /tmp/wfp/parse-duration-negative-days.patch && wc -c /tmp/wfp/parse-duration-negative-days.patch

The patch MUST be non-empty and MUST contain only your intended change. Before writing it, run `git status --short` and `git diff --cached --stat` and confirm nothing unrelated (stray scratch files, `.pyc`, editor backups, `PROBE.txt`-style files) is included; delete any such file first. Never produce an empty patch: if you are unsure of the exact upstream change, still make the best-reasoned faithful change you can.

Also write a short report file `/tmp/wfp/parse-duration-negative-days.json` containing a JSON object with keys `slug`, `status`, `files` (array of repo-relative paths you changed), `tests` (the runtests.py labels you ran and their result), and `reasoning` (2-6 sentences on what you changed and why).

## Return value

Return ONLY the structured object: slug, status ('done' if you are confident the change is complete and verified, 'partial' if implemented but unverified/uncertain, 'failed' if you could not produce a patch), and a note of at most 400 characters summarising the change (files + one-line description). Keep the note terse.

Changes you make here do NOT affect the main working directory (/workspace) or other agents. Work normally — the worktree will be cleaned up automatically if you made no changes, or preserved for review if you did.

title: 'Fixed #32269 -- Fixed parse_duration() for negative days in ISO 8601 format.'
category: bugfix
requirement: 'Developers parsing ISO 8601 durations should get correct negative timedeltas when the day component is negative. `parse_duration()` should handle values such as `-P1D`, `-P0.5D`, and `-P4DT1H` by returning the corresponding negative `timedelta` values instead of treating the sign incorrectly. This lets APIs and forms that accept ISO 8601 durations round-trip negative durations accurately.

  '

1	"""Functions to parse datetime objects."""
     2	
     3	# We're using regular expressions rather than time.strptime because:
     4	# - They provide both validation and parsing.
     5	# - They're more flexible for datetimes.
     6	# - The date/datetime/time constructors produce friendlier error messages.
     7	
     8	import datetime
     9	
    10	from django.utils.regex_helper import _lazy_re_compile
    11	from django.utils.timezone import get_fixed_timezone, utc
    12	
    13	date_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    14	    r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{1,2})-(?P<day>\d{1,2})$'
    15	)
    16	
    17	time_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    18	    r'(?P<hour>\d{1,2}):(?P<minute>\d{1,2})'
    19	    r'(?::(?P<second>\d{1,2})(?:[\.,](?P<microsecond>\d{1,6})\d{0,6})?)?'
    20	)
    21	
    22	datetime_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    23	    r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{1,2})-(?P<day>\d{1,2})'
    24	    r'[T ](?P<hour>\d{1,2}):(?P<minute>\d{1,2})'
    25	    r'(?::(?P<second>\d{1,2})(?:[\.,](?P<microsecond>\d{1,6})\d{0,6})?)?'
    26	    r'(?P<tzinfo>Z|[+-]\d{2}(?::?\d{2})?)?$'
    27	)
    28	
    29	standard_duration_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    30	    r'^'
    31	    r'(?:(?P<days>-?\d+) (days?, )?)?'
    32	    r'(?P<sign>-?)'
    33	    r'((?:(?P<hours>\d+):)(?=\d+:\d+))?'
    34	    r'(?:(?P<minutes>\d+):)?'
    35	    r'(?P<seconds>\d+)'
    36	    r'(?:[\.,](?P<microseconds>\d{1,6})\d{0,6})?'
    37	    r'$'
    38	)
    39	
    40	# Support the sections of ISO 8601 date representation that are accepted by
    41	# timedelta
    42	iso8601_duration_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    43	    r'^(?P<sign>[-+]?)'
    44	    r'P'
    45	    r'(?:(?P<days>\d+(.\d+)?)D)?'
    46	    r'(?:T'
    47	    r'(?:(?P<hours>\d+(.\d+)?)H)?'
    48	    r'(?:(?P<minutes>\d+(.\d+)?)M)?'
    49	    r'(?:(?P<seconds>\d+(.\d+)?)S)?'
    50	    r')?'
    51	    r'$'
    52	)
    53	
    54	# Support PostgreSQL's day-time interval format, e.g. "3 days 04:05:06". The
    55	# year-month and mixed intervals cannot be converted to a timedelta and thus
    56	# aren't accepted.
    57	postgres_interval_re = _lazy_re_compile(
    58	    r'^'
    59	    r'(?:(?P<days>-?\d+) (days? ?))?'
    60	    r'(?:(?P<sign>[-+])?'
    61	    r'(?P<hours>\d+):'
    62	    r'(?P<minutes>\d\d):'
    63	    r'(?P<seconds>\d\d)'
    64	    r'(?:\.(?P<microseconds>\d{1,6}))?'
    65	    r')?$'
    66	)
    67	
    68	
    69	def parse_date(value):
    70	    """Parse a string and return a datetime.date.
    71	
    72	    Raise ValueError if the input is well formatted but not a valid date.
    73	    Return None if the input isn't well formatted.
    74	    """
    75	    match = date_re.match(value)
    76	    if match:
    77	        kw = {k: int(v) for k, v in match.groupdict().items()}
    78	        return datetime.date(**kw)
    79	
    80	
    81	def parse_time(value):
    82	    """Parse a string and return a datetime.time.
    83	
    84	    This function doesn't support time zone offsets.
    85	
    86	    Raise ValueError if the input is well formatted but not a valid time.
    87	    Return None if the input isn't well formatted, in particular if it
    88	    contains an offset.
    89	    """
    90	    match = time_re.match(value)
    91	    if match:
    92	        kw = match.groupdict()
    93	        kw['microsecond'] = kw['microsecond'] and kw['microsecond'].ljust(6, '0')
    94	        kw = {k: int(v) for k, v in kw.items() if v is not None}
    95	        return datetime.time(**kw)
    96	
    97	
    98	def parse_datetime(value):
    99	    """Parse a string and return a datetime.datetime.
   100	
   101	    This function supports time zone offsets. When the input contains one,
   102	    the output uses a timezone with a fixed offset from UTC.
   103	
   104	    Raise ValueError if the input is well formatted but not a valid datetime.
   105	    Return None if the input isn't well formatted.
   106	    """
   107	    match = datetime_re.match(value)
   108	    if match:
   109	        kw = match.groupdict()
   110	        kw['microsecond'] = kw['microsecond'] and kw['microsecond'].ljust(6, '0')
   111	        tzinfo = kw.pop('tzinfo')
   112	        if tzinfo == 'Z':
   113	            tzinfo = utc
   114	        elif tzinfo is not None:
   115	            offset_mins = int(tzinfo[-2:]) if len(tzinfo) > 3 else 0
   116	            offset = 60 * int(tzinfo[1:3]) + offset_mins
   117	            if tzinfo[0] == '-':
   118	                offset = -offset
   119	            tzinfo = get_fixed_timezone(offset)
   120	        kw = {k: int(v) for k, v in kw.items() if v is not None}
   121	        kw['tzinfo'] = tzinfo
   122	        return datetime.datetime(**kw)
   123	
   124	
   125	def parse_duration(value):
   126	    """Parse a duration string and return a datetime.timedelta.
   127	
   128	    The preferred format for durations in Django is '%d %H:%M:%S.%f'.
   129	
   130	    Also supports ISO 8601 representation and PostgreSQL's day-time interval
   131	    format.
   132	    """
   133	    match = (
   134	        standard_duration_re.match(value) or
   135	        iso8601_duration_re.match(value) or
   136	        postgres_interval_re.match(value)
   137	    )
   138	    if match:
   139	        kw = match.groupdict()
   140	        sign = -1 if kw.pop('sign', '+') == '-' else 1
   141	        if kw.get('microseconds'):
   142	            kw['microseconds'] = kw['microseconds'].ljust(6, '0')
   143	        if kw.get('seconds') and kw.get('microseconds') and kw['seconds'].startswith('-'):
   144	            kw['microseconds'] = '-' + kw['microseconds']
   145	        kw = {k: float(v.replace(',', '.')) for k, v in kw.items() if v is not None}
   146	        days = datetime.timedelta(kw.pop('days', .0) or .0)
   147	        return days + sign * datetime.timedelta(**kw)
